clue.text: Saved what does come in for recycling

indicators.note: recycling breaks material down and remakes it, so the words before it are remade in another order

blocks.note: ten letters taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone praises thrift: whatever comes into the house gets recycled.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters of 'does come in' rearrange exactly into ECONOMISED.
explanation.definitionFit: To economise is to spend less, so money economised is money kept back rather than spent.

clue.text: A number of Romans in sexual revelry

indicators.note: the small number is placed inside the adjective that follows it

blocks.note: carnal means of the flesh, sexual
four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A scene of Roman debauchery, with several citizens caught up in an orgy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A number of Romans' sounds like a crowd of citizens, but it is a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: A carnival is a festive season of public merrymaking, processions and celebration, which is revelry.

clue.text: Sundry loons, for example

blocks.note: first meaning: an old word for various or several
second meaning: loons are diving water birds

explanation.walkthrough: 'Loons' looks like slang for crazy people; here it is the North American name for the birds the British call divers.
explanation.definitionFit: Divers is an archaic adjective for several or various, and divers are also a family of diving waterbirds.

clue.text: Victory comes in time for Sir Humphrey

indicators.note: one thing coming in to another sits inside it

blocks.note: a day is a period of time
V is the standard abbreviation for victory

explanation.surface: A knight's victory arrives just in time.
explanation.walkthrough: V goes inside DAY to give DAVY. Sir Humphry Davy was the chemist who invented the miners' safety lamp.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Humphry Davy, the early nineteenth-century English chemist, is identified here by his knighthood and first name.

clue.text: Betsy and her charge — unfortunately insane

definitions.note: the answer is the adjective describing these characters

indicators.note: something unfortunate has gone wrong, so the word after it is jumbled

blocks.note: Mr Dick lives in Betsy Trotwood's care in David Copperfield
taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: Betsy and the person in her care have both, sadly, lost their minds.
explanation.walkthrough: Betsy Trotwood is David Copperfield's aunt, and her charge Mr Dick is a gentle, simple-minded man, so 'insane' suits the surface too.
explanation.definitionFit: Both Betsy Trotwood and Mr Dick are characters created by Charles Dickens, so they are Dickensian figures.

clue.text: The Grauniad's road race?

blocks.note: surface reading: a running event organised by the Guardian newspaper
setter's reading: a sprint on the M1 motorway, which the error-prone paper would surely print with its spaces and digits muddled

explanation.walkthrough: The Guardian was nicknamed the Grauniad for its frequent typographical slips. M1 SPRINT run together reads as the answer, a typo.
explanation.definitionFit: A misprint is a typographical error, the very thing the Guardian's nickname mocks it for making.

clue.text: Decrepit Kentish river?

blocks.note: Kent is a county in South-East England
the Nile is the great African river

explanation.surface: An old, run-down river in Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the Nile does not flow through Kent; the joke is a 'South-East Nile'.
explanation.definitionFit: Senile describes someone weakened in body or mind by old age, which is what decrepit means.

clue.text: Pottery from Birmingham

indicators.note: the letters are taken out from inside the place name that follows

blocks.note: the third to sixth letters of the city's name

explanation.surface: Ceramics made in the Midlands city.
explanation.definitionFit: Ming is the fine porcelain made in China during the Ming dynasty, so it is a type of pottery.

clue.text: Noisy performance given daily — one with some variation

indicators.note: only some of the following word is wanted, its first part, with the rest dropped

blocks.note: a daily is a cleaning woman, also called a char
Roman numeral one
joins the pieces
taken as written before cutting

explanation.surface: A daily show that is loud and varies a little each time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' looks like 'every day' but is the British char, a cleaner. Only the first four letters of 'variation' are used.
explanation.definitionFit: A charivari is a mock serenade of banging pans and shouting, a raucous din staged outside a house.

clue.text: Lack of warmth with Ulster tribe of old

blocks.note: ice is coldness, the absence of warmth
Northern Ireland, often called Ulster

explanation.surface: An ancient Irish tribe living in the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to Ireland, but the Iceni lived in East Anglia; Boudicca was their queen.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iceni were a Celtic people of ancient Britain who rose against Roman rule, an ancient tribe.

clue.text: Sprinter fails to start is state religious establishment

indicators.note: failing to start means the opening letter is missing
one thing being in another; here the shortened word sits inside the state

blocks.note: the abbreviation for New York state
a sprinter is a runner

explanation.surface: An athlete stumbles at the start line, witnessed by state officials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' does unusual work here as the signal for putting one thing inside another; 'state' is the US state abbreviation, as common in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A nunnery is a convent, a house where a community of nuns lives under religious vows.

clue.text: Writer whose first name Cockney finds exceeding difficult to pronounce

definitions.text: Writer whose first name Cockney finds exceeding difficult to pronounce

blocks.clueFragment: Writer whose first name Cockney finds exceeding difficult to pronounce
blocks.note: surface reading: an author with a first name a Londoner would trip over
setter's reading: echoes a cake brand's slogan 'exceedingly good', and Rudyard is a mouthful for anyone dropping consonants

explanation.walkthrough: The author of The Jungle Book was named Rudyard. 'Exceeding' nods to the slogan of Mr Kipling cakes, which 'make exceedingly good cakes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rudyard Kipling was the English author of The Jungle Book and Kim, famous for his unusual first name.

clue.text: Many a bird is a thrush

blocks.note: first meaning: bird is British slang for a young woman, and this is a common woman's name
second meaning: an old and poetic name for the song thrush

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves seem to be about birds, but the first uses bird as slang for a woman, many of whom were called Mavis.
explanation.definitionFit: Mavis is a girl's name borne by many women, and mavis is also the dialect name for the song thrush.

clue.text: Season to study ten-cent book

blocks.note: to con is to study or learn by heart
a dime is the American ten-cent coin
New Testament

explanation.surface: Reading a cheap paperback through a season of study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Season' reads as a time of year but is a noun for something that flavours food.
explanation.definitionFit: A condiment is a seasoning, such as salt or mustard, added to food to flavour it.

clue.text: Needlework given as complement to Queen

blocks.note: a ship's complement is its full crew
Ellery Queen, the pen-name and detective of American mystery novels

explanation.surface: Embroidery offered as a present to go with the Queen's outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complement' looks like it means something that completes, but it is a ship's full crew.
explanation.definitionFit: Crewellery is embroidery worked in crewel, a loosely twisted worsted yarn, so it is a kind of needlework.

clue.text: Not quite the last word in hair fashion

indicators.note: not quite all of the phrase is used, so its final letter goes
the shortened piece is put in the word that follows

blocks.note: a tress is a lock of hair
the last word of something is its ending

explanation.surface: A hairstyle that is almost, but not quite, the latest thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The last word in' looks like a phrase meaning the latest fashion, but it must be split: the last word is the wordplay, 'in' the placing signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Trendiness is the quality of following the latest style, which is what being in fashion means.

clue.text: Obstacle to commission — a rise, less a/c sent in error

indicators.note: a thing done in error is done wrongly, so these letters come out in the wrong order

blocks.note: fifteen letters taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: A salesman's bonus is blocked because a pay rise, minus a wrongly sent account, went astray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Less' looks like subtraction but is simply part of the letters; a/c (account) supplies A and C.
explanation.definitionFit: Sales resistance is customers' reluctance to buy, which keeps a salesperson from earning commission on deals.

clue.text: Traditionalist Jew to quote in certain quarters

blocks.note: south, one compass point or quarter
to adduce is to cite as evidence
places the verb between the two points
east, another compass quarter

explanation.surface: Citing an orthodox Jewish source in some circles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Certain quarters' supplies two compass points, S and E, which wrap ADDUCE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sadducees were a priestly Jewish sect who held strictly to the written Law and rejected later oral tradition.

clue.text: Inventor unused to officer and other ranks

blocks.note: new means not yet used
commanding officer
joins the pieces
the men are soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: An inventor with no military experience is sent to the officers and men.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Newcomen built the first practical steam engine in 1712.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Newcomen invented the atmospheric steam engine used to pump water from mines, so he was an inventor.

clue.text: Leading director, keen and economical

indicators.note: what leads comes first, so only the opening letter of the next word is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of this word
avid means eager, keen
joins the pieces
lean means sparing, without waste

explanation.surface: A top film-maker described as keen and thrifty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Director' does double duty: it is part of the definition and also gives its first letter. David Lean directed Lawrence of Arabia.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir David Lean, maker of Lawrence of Arabia and Doctor Zhivago, was one of Britain's foremost film directors.

clue.text: In depraved situation Jack's likely to succeed  …

indicators.note: the sailor is placed in the description of a base situation

blocks.note: a depraved situation is a vile one
a jack is a sailor, and an AB is an able seaman

explanation.surface: A man called Jack, caught up in corruption, is tipped for success.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack (also jack tar) is crossword shorthand for a sailor, AB.
explanation.definitionFit: A viable plan or venture is workable and capable of succeeding, so it is likely to succeed.

clue.text: Having planted seed, therefore had to get married

blocks.note: so means therefore
wed means married

explanation.surface: A man who got a woman pregnant was therefore forced into marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a shotgun wedding; 'planted seed' is meant literally, a gardener's sowing.
explanation.definitionFit: Sowed is the past tense of sow, to scatter seed in the ground, which is to have planted seed.

clue.text: …  and cast out drink

indicators.note: the word is spread out to make room in its middle for the other

blocks.note: to shy is to throw or cast
taken as written

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: a sailor who throws away his drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots carry the sentence on from the previous clue. Shandy is beer mixed with lemonade, a British pub staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Shandy is a drink of beer mixed with lemonade or ginger beer, popular in British pubs.

clue.text: Slow part of service?

blocks.note: first meaning: happening little by little
second meaning: an antiphon sung between the readings at Mass

explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' suggests waiters or tennis, but it is a church service; the gradual is sung between Epistle and Gospel.
explanation.definitionFit: Gradual means proceeding by small degrees, and the gradual is also a response sung during the Mass.

clue.text: College servant supply some of the means to get plastered

indicators.note: only some of the next phrase's answer is used, the tail being cut off

blocks.note: gypsum is the mineral used to make plaster

explanation.surface: A college's staff are kept supplied with plastering materials, or with drink.
explanation.walkthrough: A gyp is a college servant at Cambridge, so a supply of them is GYPS; 'plastered' also hints at drunkenness. GYPSUM loses its last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Gyps are the male college servants at Cambridge and Durham, so a supply of such servants is several gyps.

clue.text: Man in service used to bore at length about nothing

indicators.note: the phrase goes about, around, the zero

blocks.note: to drag on is to continue tediously
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A serviceman who goes on and on about nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used to' looks like part of the wordplay (formerly) but is just a link joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A dragoon is a cavalry soldier, originally a mounted infantryman, so he is a man in military service.

clue.text: Attraction of the lottery

blocks.note: first meaning: something that pulls in crowds
second meaning: the event where winning numbers are picked

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as the appeal of playing the lottery, but it is two meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A draw is a feature that pulls in the public, and also the random selection of winning tickets in a lottery.

clue.text: Heart-throb turns up at college

indicators.note: turning the next word round makes it read backwards in this down-the-page sense

blocks.note: taken as written
joins the pieces
the London School of Economics

explanation.surface: A dreamy idol makes an appearance at a university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart-throb' suggests a pin-up but means the throb of the heart.
explanation.definitionFit: A pulse is the rhythmic throbbing of the arteries as the heart beats.

clue.text: Forward to study manure

blocks.note: to read a subject is to study it
to dress land is to spread manure on it

explanation.surface: A student told to learn about fertiliser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forward' looks like an adverb but is the verb for sending mail on.
explanation.definitionFit: To readdress a letter is to put a new address on it so it is sent on, which is to forward it.
